books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text:
Original secondary passage, written for this question from the grounding books:

In the cities of the Gilded Age, immigrants balanced two pulls. Foreign-language newspapers such as the Yiddish-language Jewish Daily Forward and the Italian-language Il Progresso Italo-Americano served whole neighborhoods, and Little Italy and the Jewish Lower East Side of New York grew into worlds of their own, with grocery stores, savings banks, choruses, and political clubs.

At the same time, millions of newcomers, mostly young men, worked part of the year in the United States and spent the rest at home; they were called “birds of passage” for their seasonal coming and going.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage, written for this question from Barron’s Premium 2027 Chapter 8 (Topic 6.9), 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, and Princeton Review, Chapter 10.

stem: The term “birds of passage” in the passage refers to immigrants who

options.text: settled permanently in one American city
options.misconception: Describes permanent settlers, the opposite of seasonal migrants.

options.text: never left their home countries at all
options.misconception: Describes people who never came, not people who came and went.

options.text: moved west to claim farmland under the Homestead Act
options.misconception: Names western farmers instead of seasonal city workers.

options.text: worked here part of the year and then went home

rationales.A: Permanent settlers stayed put. Birds of passage came and went with the seasons.
rationales.B: Birds of passage did leave home: they worked in the United States for part of each year.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about farmland or the Homestead Act. These migrants worked for wages and went home.
rationales.D: The passage says millions of newcomers, mostly young men, worked part of the year in the United States and spent the rest at home, and were called birds of passage for their seasonal coming and going.
rationales.general:
Follow the definition the passage gives for the nickname.
1. The nickname belongs to millions of newcomers, mostly young men.
2. They worked part of the year in the United States.
3. They spent the rest of the year at home.
4. So the name fits seasonal coming and going, not settling or staying home.
Remember: a nickname in a passage is defined by the sentence that introduces it.
